Iran International

Around 650 million cubic meters of groundwater are extracted annually from approximately 1,200 wells to supply Tehran and its surrounding areas, Ali Beitollahi, head of the earthquake and risk assessment department at Iran's Road, Housing and Urban Development Research Center, said.

Unlike agricultural wells, which may operate for only a few hours a day depending on seasonal demand, urban water supplies require year-round extraction, he said.

The continued pumping of groundwater in areas already affected by subsidence is lowering water tables and degrading water quality, Beitollahi said.

Buildings, gas pipelines, water networks and sewage systems could suffer structural damage as the ground sinks, he warned, adding that population density and earthquake risks must also be considered when assessing the danger.

Iran's largest subsidence zones overlap with its most densely populated metropolitan areas, particularly Tehran and neighboring Karaj, followed by Isfahan, Beitollahi said.

The entire Isfahan metropolitan area is exposed to subsidence risks, he added.

The scale of the problem has expanded nationwide. Land affected by subsidence increased tenfold over eight years, from approximately 10,000 to 100,000 square kilometers, Reza Shahbazi, deputy head of Iran's Geological Survey, said in September.

A parliamentary research report cited by Shargh newspaper in June warned that subsidence had reached a critical stage, with around half of Iran's population living in affected areas.

Population concentration strains water supplies

Around 40% of Iran's population lives within 100 kilometers of 10 major population centers, including Tehran and Mashhad, according to Beitollahi.

The concentration of jobs, infrastructure and services in these areas has increased demand for water, energy and food, placing further pressure on groundwater reserves.

Water conservation alone cannot resolve the problem because of the scale of population concentration, Beitollahi said.

He called for creating employment opportunities and improving living conditions elsewhere in Iran to reduce pressure on Tehran and Karaj, warning that continued population concentration would make future water supplies unsustainable.
